hook: Choose the forward-rate volatility. No-arbitrage then constrains the curve's drift.
narration: In many short-rate models, one number has to generate an entire yield curve. Heath, Jarrow, and Morton flipped the starting point: model the whole forward curve across maturities. Once you choose how its volatility factors move, no-arbitrage constrains the risk-neutral drift. The HJM framework is foundational to modern arbitrage-free forward-rate models; the late-1990s LIBOR Market Model is a direct descendant, though not every stochastic-rate model comes from HJM. This interactive curve uses synthetic loadings and shocks, not market calibration.

shots.cue: Show the editable forward curve and explain that each point is a maturity.
Change the volatility shape, then compare the one-factor and two-factor paths.
Send a synthetic shock to the five-year forward and watch the curve respond.
Show the risk-neutral drift condition and clarify that HJM does not determine volatility or absorb every short-rate model.

carousel: A short rate is one number; a forward curve is a whole maturity structure.
HJM models that whole curve directly.
Choose the volatility factors, and the risk-neutral no-arbitrage condition constrains the drift.
HJM is foundational to the modern arbitrage-free forward-rate framework; BGM/LMM is a direct descendant, not proof that every rate model is HJM-derived.
